author: FP&A Analyst
comment: An unplanned client project was won in late March and delivered inside April; external production was booked at short-notice premium rates. Together with the matching revenue line the net margin impact is slightly negative. Change-order discipline flagged to the project director.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Unbudgeted revenue from the same late-won April project; see the matching COGS variance. Recognized on delivery.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: November events were delivered with in-house crew and staging stock instead of the subcontracting assumed in budget; Q4 freight was also renegotiated. Genuine savings, not a timing shift.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: A client brought part of its September roadshow forward into July. Timing between months rather than new business; the September shortfall stayed within tolerance.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Two platform go-lives slipped from January into February on client-side content delays. Revenue is recognized on delivery, so January carries the gap; both projects were invoiced in February.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: A brand activation sold for early 2025 was pulled into October at the client's request. The matching cost variance appears on the COGS line the same month.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Production costs of the pulled-forward October activation; see the matching revenue variance.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: External development spend paused over the year-end delivery freeze and resumed in February, alongside the two go-lives that slipped on the revenue line. This recurs every holiday season; budget phasing to be corrected in the next cycle.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: One retainer client commissioned an out-of-cycle campaign microsite in an otherwise quiet August.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Two institutional clients pushed their October milestone invoicing into November after a budget-cycle approval delay on their side. Timing only.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Delivery costs of the two milestones that slipped into November were held back with them; see the matching revenue variance. Timing only.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Contractor spend deferred during the summer staffing gap on the delivery bench; caught up from September.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Freelance day rates paused over the same summer gap as the deferred contractor work; see the matching external production variance.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Freelance motion designers booked to cover a vacant post through the November campaign peak. The permanent hire started in January.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Freelance bookings paused with the two platform go-lives that slipped into February; see the matching revenue variance.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: January carried final supplier invoices for a December 2023 conference that arrived after the prior-year cut-off. Timing across the year-end, no change to the full-year run-rate.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: The June conference was held in a client-owned venue instead of the hired venue assumed in budget; venue and catering pass-through came in under plan. A saving, not timing.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Two May engagements ran on the in-house registration platform rather than the external provider budgeted for them; supplier spend under plan. A saving, not timing.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: The September summit required additional security screening and accreditation staffing imposed by the host ministry after the budget was set; only part of it could be recharged.

author: FP&A Analyst
comment: Fewer freelance crew days in a light January build schedule; the permanent technical team covered the work. Volume, consistent with the month's activity.
